cues.text: Let us turn now to a topic that sits at the heart of modern information technology practice: data ownership, stewardship and consent.
We begin with a question that sounds simple.
Who owns data?
Many people assume that ownership works like owning a laptop or a car.
You hold it, you paid for it, so you decide everything about it.
But the source material is careful to say that data ownership is not a simple property label.
Instead, several different parties have different kinds of claims, and those claims are layered on top of one another.
First, individuals.
Individuals have privacy and data-subject rights.
A data subject is simply the person whom the data is about.
Those rights belong to that person, even when someone else is holding the records.
Second, organisations.
An organisation may hold records, and it may also have intellectual property interests in its systems or in compilations of data.
A compilation is a collected, organised set of information.
So an organisation can have a genuine interest in the database it built, without that meaning it owns the individuals' rights in the personal details inside it.
Third, processors.
A processor is a party that handles data under instructions.
Think of a cloud provider or a payroll service that works on data for another organisation.
The processor does not decide for itself what to do with the data; it acts on the instructions it is given.
Fourth, contracts and law.
These allocate rights and duties among all of these parties.
So the answer to who may do what with data depends on the contract, on the law, and on the role each party plays.
Now notice an important warning in the source.
Possessing records, or paying for storage, does not permit unrestricted secondary use.
Secondary use means using data for a purpose beyond the one for which it was originally collected.
Suppose a company stores customer records and pays a hosting fee every month.
That does not give it the freedom to use those records for any new purpose it likes.
Holding data and being free to do anything with it are two different things.
This leads us to data stewardship.
Stewardship is responsible management of data.
The source says it involves a clear purpose, clear access rules, data quality, retention, and oversight.
Let me say those again as a checklist.
Purpose: why do we hold this data?
Access: who may see or use it?
Quality: is it accurate and kept up to date?
Retention: how long do we keep it?
And oversight: who checks that all of this is actually being done?
A steward, in other words, is not an owner with unlimited freedom, but a caretaker with responsibilities.
Let us move to consent.
According to the source, consent is meaningful where it is informed, specific, freely given, unambiguous, and withdrawable as required.
Let us take each in turn.
Informed means the person understands what they are agreeing to.
Specific means the agreement relates to a particular purpose, not a vague general permission.
Freely given means the person has a real choice and is not pressured or forced.
Unambiguous means it is clear that the person agreed.
And withdrawable, as required, means the person can take their consent back where the rules call for that.
How do we make consent informed?
The source tells us to explain what is collected, why it is collected, with whom it is shared, how long it is retained, and what the consequences are.
Those five points are a useful template for any notice you write.
The source also says to separate necessary service processing from optional advertising or profiling.
Some processing is needed to deliver the service the person asked for.
Other processing, such as advertising or building a profile of someone's behaviour, is optional.
These should not be mixed together.
Use accessible notices, layered explanations, and easy withdrawal.
A layered explanation gives a short, simple summary first, with more detail available for those who want it.
Another rule: do not bundle unrelated permissions into compulsory acceptance.
In other words, you should not force a person to accept, say, advertising tracking as the price of using a basic service, if the two are unrelated.
Then comes a very important qualification.
Consent is only one possible lawful basis for processing.
A lawful basis is the legal justification for handling personal data.
The source says that a valid legal basis, plus additional conditions for sensitive data, is essential even when consent is inappropriate.
So do not assume that consent is always the answer.
Sometimes another basis is the right one, and sensitive data carries extra conditions on top.
Be careful here: the source does not name which other bases exist, so we will not guess.
The point to hold on to is that consent is one option among possible bases, and some form of valid legal basis is always required.
Now look at the table that accompanies this section.
It has two columns.
The left column is headed "Bad pattern" and the right column is headed "Better design." Let us walk through it row by row.
Row one.
The bad pattern is preselected optional tracking.
The better design is genuine opt-in where consent is used.
So instead of ticking the box for the user, let the user make the choice.
Row two.
The bad pattern is a long unexplained notice.
The better design is a layered, plain-language explanation.
Row three.
The bad pattern is one button for all unrelated purposes.
The better design is granular choices, meaning separate options for separate purposes.
Row four.
The bad pattern is hard-to-find deletion or export.
The better design is an accessible rights workflow, so people can easily exercise their rights.
Row five.
The bad pattern is collecting full raw biometrics unnecessarily.
Biometrics are measurements of the body, such as fingerprints or face scans.
The better design is to minimise, and use appropriate alternatives.
Next, the consent receipt.
A consent receipt is a record of a person's consent.
The source says it records the version, the purposes, the selection, the time, and the relevant identity or context.
Version tells you which wording the person saw.
Purposes tell you what they agreed to.
Selection tells you what they chose.
Time tells you when.
And identity or context tells you who and in what setting.
But there is a caution: do not store more data than necessary to prove consent.
A record meant to protect privacy should not itself become a source of excess data.
What happens when someone withdraws consent?
The source says withdrawal should stop consent-based processing prospectively.
Prospectively means going forward from that point.
This is subject to lawful exceptions and other applicable obligations.
And importantly, withdrawal does not automatically make prior lawful processing unlawful.
What was done properly before the withdrawal is not retroactively turned into a violation simply because the person later changed their mind.
The source also asks us to distinguish three ideas that are often confused: purpose limitation, retention, and data minimisation.
Purpose limitation concerns using data only for the purposes it was collected for.
Retention concerns how long data is kept.
Data minimisation concerns collecting and holding only what is necessary.
They are related, but they answer different questions: why, how long, and how much.
Finally, the data lifecycle.
The source describes it as a sequence: collect, then validate and store, then process and use, then share, then archive or retain, and finally delete or appropriately anonymise.
Anonymise means altering data so that individuals can no longer be identified, and the source says "appropriately," so it must be done properly.
At each stage, the source says we should assign owners, permissions, legal basis, controls and review.
That means for every stage someone is responsible, access is defined, a legal basis exists, safeguards are in place, and the arrangement is reviewed.
We must also honour applicable rights: access, correction, portability, deletion, objection, and other rights.
Access is seeing your data.
Correction is fixing errors.
Portability is receiving your data in a form you can move elsewhere.
Deletion is removal.
And objection is the right to object to certain processing.
One practical point: retention applies to logs, exports, vendors and backups, as well as to primary records.
It is easy to delete the main database entry and forget the copies sitting in a log file, an exported spreadsheet, a vendor's system, or a backup.
And lastly, consider what happens when an individual requests deletion.
The source says to identify exceptions, such as required medical records.
Then explain the decision to the person, and delete unnecessary copies.
So deletion is not always total.
Some records may have to be kept, but you must say why, and anything not required should still be removed.
To bring it together: ownership is layered, not absolute.
Stewardship means responsible care.
Consent must be genuine, but it is only one possible lawful basis.
And across the whole lifecycle, from collection to deletion, every stage needs clear responsibility, a legal basis, and respect for the rights of the person the data is about.
